screens.title: Introduction to Materials and Shaders
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this short module you will learn how materials turn geometry into believable surfaces, why shaders calculate how light behaves on those surfaces, and how Blender’s Principled BSDF gives you a practical, physically-based workflow. Materials are the collection of properties that define color, shininess, transparency, and how light scatters. Textures are images you feed into a material to add fine detail such as patterns or bump information. The Shader Editor is the node-based workspace where these relationships are built and adjusted. When you follow the hands-on activity in this chapter, you’ll create three distinct materials — a polished plastic, a brushed metal, and a rough stone — and see how the same sphere reads very differently under varied values for Metallic and Roughness. We’ll also cover common beginner mistakes, such as using fractional metallic values for non-metals and neglecting PBR principles that game engines expect. By the end, you’ll know which settings to tweak for predictable results in game pipelines and how to keep node setups efficient for performance. Ready to explore the parameters that give your models life?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introduction
Introduction to Materials and Shaders
How materials define appearance and why Principled BSDF is the go-to PBR shader.

Materials are the skin of your model — they tell Blender how to color, reflect, and scatter light. The Shader Editor is where you connect textures and shader nodes to the Material Output that renders the surface. This lesson focuses on the fundamental controls that shape most real-world materials.

In this lesson
Create simple PBR materials and learn key Principled BSDF settings.
Coming up
Use the Shader Editor and avoid common mistakes with Metallic and Roughness.
Outcome
Export-friendly, optimized materials suitable for game engines.
Visual overview
Material properties connect to the Principled BSDF node which outputs to Material Output.
Base Color
Primary tint; often desaturated before layering textures.
Metallic
0 for non-metals, 1 for metals. Avoid intermediate values for real materials.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide your practice as you work in the Shader Editor. First, you will learn to distinguish materials from textures: materials are collections of properties and instructions that govern light interaction, while textures are image inputs that provide surface detail. Second, you will understand the purpose and core settings of the Principled BSDF shader so you can predict how changes to Base Color, Metallic, Specular, and Roughness will affect appearance. Third, you will apply and adjust these properties on simple geometry to achieve targeted looks, like shiny plastic or brushed metal. Finally, you will learn why PBR workflows matter for game development and how keeping node setups efficient helps performance. Each objective pairs a practical action with a reason: you won’t just move sliders, you’ll also learn when a value is appropriate for a real-world material and how that maps into game engines. As you practice the hands-on steps, verify competency by producing three materials and comparing their behavior in Material Preview. These objectives set clear, testable outcomes so your work translates reliably into games.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and PBR
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide gives you a practice roadmap and clarifies why PBR matters. Practically, you will open the Shader Editor, create a new material on a UV sphere, and tweak the Principled BSDF sliders to reach specific looks. You will practice by making a polished plastic, brushed metal, and rough stone; each example trains a different idea: low roughness for sharp reflections, metallic flagged at one for metals, and desaturated base color when layering textures. PBR matters because it standardizes how light and materials behave across different engines and lighting environments. That means a material you create in Blender is more likely to look consistent when moved to a game engine if it adheres to PBR practice. A common misconception is that tweaking only Base Color is enough — in reality, Metallic and Roughness drastically change the same color’s response to light. Your milestone is to produce three distinct materials and inspect them in Material Preview. If they read correctly under varied lighting, you have a PBR-ready workflow.

Practice steps and why PBR matters

screens.title: What is a Material vs a Texture?
screens.narratorSegment: A material is the set of properties and instructions that define how a surface interacts with light: its color response, reflectivity, transparency, and scattering behavior. A texture is usually an image file that supplies specific data to a material — for example, a color map for detail, a normal map for small-surface bumps, or a roughness map that varies micro-surface scattering. Understanding this separation changes how you build assets: textures provide surface detail and variation, while materials determine the core physical behavior. For instance, a single material with a base color can look flat and synthetic; add a texture that encodes fabric weave or stone grain and the surface gains realism because light can vary across the surface. A common misconception is to treat textures as materials; beginners sometimes set every visual change as a separate material instead of driving variation with textures and parameter maps. That creates more material slots and can bloat performance in game engines. In practice, you’ll often use one material per logical surface type and feed multiple texture maps into the Principled BSDF. Ask yourself: does this change require a different physical response, or just a pattern? That question guides efficient, export-friendly designs.

keyIdea.title: Definition takeaway
keyIdea.text: Materials define physical response; textures supply surface detail. Use textures to add variety, not to multiply materials unnecessarily.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Material vs Texture
Material
A collection of properties and shader logic that define light interaction and final appearance.
  • • Controls reflectivity, roughness, metalness, transparency.
  • • Outputs to Material Output node for rendering.
  • • Often shared across many objects to save resources.
Key Takeaway

Prefer one optimized material per surface type; use textures to give per-pixel variation.

Texture
An image or map that feeds data into a material, such as base color, normals, or roughness variation.
  • • Adds detail without changing material logic.
  • • Can be packed into multiple channels for efficiency.
  • • Drives micro-variation that makes surfaces believable.
Example: a single leather material uses a color texture for grain, a normal map for small bumps, and a roughness map for shiny patches caused by wear.

screens.title: Using the Shader Editor
screens.narratorSegment: The Shader Editor is Blender’s node-based environment for building materials. When you select an object and open the Shader Editor, you’ll typically see a Principled BSDF node connected to a Material Output node by default. Think of the Material Output as the final destination for color and surface properties — anything you want to affect the render must connect to it. The power of nodes is that you can insert textures, mix shaders, and add math nodes to control values procedurally. Practically, create a new material from the Material Properties tab or directly within the Shader Editor using the New button. If the object has no material, adding one automatically creates the default Principled BSDF and Material Output pair, so you can start tweaking. A common mistake is editing the wrong object or working in the wrong material slot; always confirm the selected object’s material is active in the editor. For performance, keep node trees as compact as possible for game assets. As an exercise, create a simple node chain: Image Texture → Base Color input of Principled BSDF → Material Output, then preview in Material Preview mode to see immediate results. How would you reduce node complexity for game export?

keyIdea.title: Shader Editor takeaway
keyIdea.text: The node graph feeds Material Output; confirm active object and simplify node trees for performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Shader Editor
Node architecture
Material Output receives shader results. Principled BSDF is the main node that computes appearance.
# Example node chain (conceptual)
Image Texture -> Base Color (Principled BSDF)
Principled BSDF -> Surface (Material Output)
# For normal detail:
Normal Map -> Normal (Principled BSDF)
Tip: Use Image Texture nodes for maps and group repeated node setups into node groups to keep graphs tidy and efficient for export.
Common mistakes
  • • Editing a different material slot than the selected object — always verify the active material.
  • • Overcomplicating node graphs for realtime assets — aim for simplicity and texture-driven variation.
  • • Forgetting Material Output — disconnected nodes render nothing.
Pro tip

Group reusable node patterns and name your node groups for quick reuse across assets.

screens.title: Principled BSDF Parameters — Overview
screens.narratorSegment: The Principled BSDF consolidates common physical material controls into a single, intuitive node. Base Color sets the primary tint and is often driven by a texture for detailed surfaces. Metallic is a binary-like property: 0 for non-metals like plastic or wood, 1 for metals like steel; using fractional metallic values on non-metals is a common beginner error and can create physically inconsistent results. Specular controls the intensity of highlights and for PBR workflows it is usually left near the default for non-metals because the shader already models energy-conserving reflections; it has little effect on metals. Roughness governs microfacet spread: low roughness creates sharp, mirror-like reflections, high roughness produces diffuse, matte surfaces. These parameters interact: the same Base Color will read very differently when Metallic flips from 0 to 1 or when Roughness changes from 0.1 to 0.8. When designing for games, tune Roughness to convey material wear and polish, and keep Metallic strictly at 0 or 1 for realistic results. A useful mental model: Base Color = paint, Metallic = material class, Roughness = polish level. Which parameter would you adjust first to turn a matte plastic into a glossy painted car?

keyIdea.title: Parameter summary
keyIdea.text: Base Color paints the surface, Metallic sets metal vs non-metal behavior, Specular tunes highlight intensity, Roughness controls reflection sharpness.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Principled BSDF
Parameter comparison
Base Color
Primary tint; usually fed by an image texture for detail.
Metallic
0 for dielectrics, 1 for metals. Avoid mid-values for realistic metals.
Specular
Intensity of highlights; often left near default for non-metals in PBR.
Roughness
0 = mirror, 1 = fully diffuse. Controls sharpness and spread of reflections.
Concrete examples
  • • Polished plastic: Base Color bright, Metallic 0, Roughness ~0.2.
  • • Brushed metal: Base Color dark grey, Metallic 1, Roughness ~0.6.
  • • Rough stone: Base Color brown-grey, Metallic 0, Roughness ~0.8.
Key Takeaway

Tweak Roughness first for finish, set Metallic as a class, and use Base Color textures for detail.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create a Polished Plastic Material
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a simple process to produce a polished plastic material that reads clearly in material preview. Start by creating a UV Sphere in the 3D Viewport and switching a pane to the Shader Editor. With the sphere selected, click New to create a material — Blender will provide a Principled BSDF connected to Material Output. Set Base Color to a vibrant blue and keep it somewhat saturated so the color reads under different lights. Set Metallic to zero because plastic is a non-metal. Reduce Roughness to about 0.2 to achieve a glossy, polished surface while maintaining subtle micro-variation that prevents a perfect mirror. Leave Specular at the default for PBR consistency. Inspect the result in Material Preview mode, move the viewport light, and notice how reflections sharpen as Roughness decreases. A typical misconception is to push Metallic up to make the highlight brighter — that will change the reflection model and make the surface behave like metal rather than painted plastic. After this exercise, try nudging Roughness slightly to see how much it affects perceived gloss without changing Base Color.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Polished Plastic
Step-by-step
1. Add a UV Sphere (Shift + A → Mesh → UV Sphere).
2. Open Shader Editor and click New.
3. Set Base Color to blue (Hex: #0000FF).
4. Set Metallic = 0.
5. Set Roughness = 0.2.
6. View in Material Preview mode and rotate the light.
This exact sequence trains the feel of how Roughness alters reflection sharpness while Metallic changes reflection type.
Example: outcome
A polished toy car or plastic helmet typically uses these settings: non-metallic base with low roughness to show clear reflections without being mirror-like.
Common mistake

Raising Metallic to make highlights brighter converts the object into metal; avoid that when making paint or plastic.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create a Brushed Metal Material
screens.narratorSegment: To make a believable brushed metal, start from a duplicated UV sphere so you can compare materials side by side. Create a new material for the duplicate rather than reusing the plastic material. Set Base Color to a dark grey — metals base color is often muted because real metals get their color from reflections rather than diffused pigment. Set Metallic to 1 to ensure the shader uses metal reflection behavior; this is critical because metals reflect the environment and tint reflections by their base color. Increase Roughness to around 0.6 to simulate a brushed surface that scatters reflections while retaining some directional highlights. Optionally add a subtle noise texture into Roughness or Normal input to break uniformity, but be mindful of node complexity for game assets. Remember the common trap: using metallic fractions for non-metals. Metals are typically flagged as fully metallic. After applying these values, move the HDRI or light to see how the object reflects its environment; that reflection behavior is the primary cue that a surface is metallic. How would adding a normal map change the perception of brushed direction?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Brushed Metal
Quick steps
  1. Duplicate the sphere and create a new material.
  2. Set Base Color to dark grey (Hex: #333333).
  3. Set Metallic = 1.
  4. Set Roughness ≈ 0.6; add directional normal map for brushed streaks if needed.
Example: outcome
A kitchen appliance or metal trim reads as metal primarily because of environment reflections. The base color tints those reflections subtly.
Warning

Do not use intermediate metallic values for metals; set metallic to 1 for realistic metal response.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create a Rough Stone Material
screens.narratorSegment: Create a rough stone material to practice diffuse and high-roughness behavior. Duplicate your sphere again and assign a new material. Set Base Color to a brownish-grey to represent rock, and set Metallic to zero because stone is non-metallic. Increase Roughness to about 0.8 to scatter reflections and give a dull appearance. To add realism, use a texture or procedural noise to modulate the roughness channel so some areas appear slightly shinier where the stone is worn. Normal maps are especially valuable for stone because they add surface detail that catches light at grazing angles. Keep Specular near default for non-metals. A common misconception is that increasing Roughness hides geometry detail — it changes reflections but you still need normal or displacement information to convey bumps and cracks. Inspect the result in Material Preview and rotate the light to verify the surface reads as matte and granular. If you wanted a wet patch, which parameter would you change and in what direction? Hands-on: Create a Rough Stone Material means rough stone: base color earthy, metallic 0, roughness high (~0.8); use normal maps to convey micro-detail.. In practical terms, using roughness and base color for non-metallic, diffuse surfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Rough Stone
Quick recipe
  • • Base Color: brown-grey (Hex: #665544)
  • • Metallic: 0
  • • Roughness: ~0.8; blend a noise texture into Roughness for variety
  • • Add Normal map for bumps
Example & check
Stone feels convincing when reflections are muted and surface detail is visible through normals. To simulate wetness, lower Roughness locally and increase specular response on those patches.
Key Takeaway

High roughness plus normal detail produces believable coarse materials; use localized roughness changes for wet or polished areas.

screens.title: Practical Node Example (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s walk through a compact, practical node setup you will use repeatedly. Start with the Principled BSDF connected to Material Output — that’s the baseline. Add an Image Texture node for Base Color and connect it to Base Color input. For surface detail, add a Normal Map node: load a normal texture into an Image Texture, set its color space to non-color, plug it into the Normal Map node, and connect that into the Principled BSDF Normal input. To vary gloss, add a second Image Texture for Roughness and feed it into the Roughness input. If you want efficiency, pack multiple grayscale maps into channels of a single image — for example, roughness in the red channel and ambient occlusion in green — then use a Separate RGB node to split channels before feeding them where needed. Beginners often forget to set image nodes to the correct color space; normal maps must be non-color or they will render incorrectly. This simple chain gives a tightly controlled PBR material that is straightforward to optimize and export for game engines. Practical Node Example (Conceptual) means image texture → principled inputs (base color, normal, roughness) → material output; set correct color spaces and pack maps when possible.. In practical terms, a simple node chain to create textured pbr materials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Node Example
Conceptual node walkthrough
# Conceptual node connections
Image Texture (Base Color) -> Base Color (Principled BSDF)
Image Texture (Normal, non-color) -> Normal Map -> Normal (Principled BSDF)
Image Texture (Roughness, non-color) -> Roughness (Principled BSDF)

screens.title: Common Beginner Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners frequently make a small set of recurring mistakes that reduce realism or complicate export. First, using fractional Metallic values for non-metals — metals are either metallic or not. A plastic or painted surface should use Metallic = 0. Second, ignoring PBR energy-conserving defaults such as Specular and expecting to fix everything with Base Color; Specular is tuned by the Principled shader and often works best left near defaults for dielectrics. Third, failing to set correct image color spaces: normal maps must be non-color, while base color textures need sRGB. Fourth, creating many tiny materials instead of using textures to vary a single material; that increases draw calls and reduces performance in real-time engines. Finally, overcomplicating node graphs for realtime assets; keep nodes simple and reuse node groups. The remedy is to adopt PBR habits: treat Metallic as a class flag, use Roughness to control finish, pack maps efficiently, and preview your materials under different lighting. A quick test is to import your material into the engine or simulate different HDRIs to confirm consistent behavior. screens.title: PBR and Game Engine Compatibility
screens.narratorSegment: Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, models material response to light using physical principles so materials behave consistently across lighting conditions and engines. The Principled BSDF is built for PBR workflows, which is why it’s commonly used for game assets: it reduces guesswork and helps Blender materials translate predictably into engines like Unity or Unreal. This consistency matters because a material that relies on ad-hoc shader tricks may look good in one scene but break under different lighting or in another engine. PBR parameters — Base Color, Metallic, Roughness, Normal — map directly to game engine inputs, which streamlines export. For performance, avoid complex procedural setups when baking to textures is an option: bake maps such as base color, normal, and roughness, then use those textures in the engine. A misconception is that PBR removes artistic control; in fact, it gives predictable control, letting you concentrate on art direction while ensuring technical compatibility. As you prepare assets for games, ask whether your material will need to be baked and whether node complexity interferes with that process. screens.title: Activity Walkthrough and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: After creating your three materials, run a quick verification checklist to confirm PBR readiness and engine compatibility. First, inspect Base Color textures: ensure they are not overly saturated and that color profiles are correct. Second, check Metallic values: metals should be set to one and non-metals to zero. Third, preview the model under different HDRI setups or lighting rigs to verify reflections and roughness behavior remain plausible. Fourth, open each image texture and set color space correctly — normal maps need non-color, base color should remain sRGB. Fifth, review node complexity: can procedural detail be baked into textures instead of computed in real time? Finally, perform a simple export or bake test: bake base color, normal, and roughness into files and reassign them in a fresh material to compare the baked result with your live nodes. This test tells you whether your material can be simplified for engines. A common pitfall is skipping the baked test and discovering later that a complex node tree cannot be reproduced efficiently in the game pipeline. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this short module you will learn how materials turn geometry into believable surfaces, why shaders calculate how light behaves on those surfaces, and how Blender’s Principled BSDF gives you a practical, physically-based workflow. Materials are the collection of properties that define color, shininess, transparency, and how light scatters. Textures are images you feed into a material to add fine detail such as patterns or bump information. The Shader Editor is the node-based workspace where these relationships are built and adjusted. When you follow the hands-on activity in this chapter, you’ll create three distinct materials — a polished plastic, a brushed metal, and a rough stone — and see how the same sphere reads very differently under varied values for Metallic and Roughness. We’ll also cover common beginner mistakes, such as using fractional metallic values for non-metals and neglecting PBR principles that game engines expect. By the end, you’ll know which settings to tweak for predictable results in game pipelines and how to keep node setups efficient for performance. Ready to explore the parameters that give your models life?

These objectives will guide your practice as you work in the Shader Editor. First, you will learn to distinguish materials from textures: materials are collections of properties and instructions that govern light interaction, while textures are image inputs that provide surface detail. Second, you will understand the purpose and core settings of the Principled BSDF shader so you can predict how changes to Base Color, Metallic, Specular, and Roughness will affect appearance. Third, you will apply and adjust these properties on simple geometry to achieve targeted looks, like shiny plastic or brushed metal. Finally, you will learn why PBR workflows matter for game development and how keeping node setups efficient helps performance. Each objective pairs a practical action with a reason: you won’t just move sliders, you’ll also learn when a value is appropriate for a real-world material and how that maps into game engines. As you practice the hands-on steps, verify competency by producing three materials and comparing their behavior in Material Preview. These objectives set clear, testable outcomes so your work translates reliably into games.

This second objectives slide gives you a practice roadmap and clarifies why PBR matters. Practically, you will open the Shader Editor, create a new material on a UV sphere, and tweak the Principled BSDF sliders to reach specific looks. You will practice by making a polished plastic, brushed metal, and rough stone; each example trains a different idea: low roughness for sharp reflections, metallic flagged at one for metals, and desaturated base color when layering textures. PBR matters because it standardizes how light and materials behave across different engines and lighting environments. That means a material you create in Blender is more likely to look consistent when moved to a game engine if it adheres to PBR practice. A common misconception is that tweaking only Base Color is enough — in reality, Metallic and Roughness drastically change the same color’s response to light. Your milestone is to produce three distinct materials and inspect them in Material Preview. If they read correctly under varied lighting, you have a PBR-ready workflow.

A material is the set of properties and instructions that define how a surface interacts with light: its color response, reflectivity, transparency, and scattering behavior. A texture is usually an image file that supplies specific data to a material — for example, a color map for detail, a normal map for small-surface bumps, or a roughness map that varies micro-surface scattering. Understanding this separation changes how you build assets: textures provide surface detail and variation, while materials determine the core physical behavior. For instance, a single material with a base color can look flat and synthetic; add a texture that encodes fabric weave or stone grain and the surface gains realism because light can vary across the surface. A common misconception is to treat textures as materials; beginners sometimes set every visual change as a separate material instead of driving variation with textures and parameter maps. That creates more material slots and can bloat performance in game engines. In practice, you’ll often use one material per logical surface type and feed multiple texture maps into the Principled BSDF. Ask yourself: does this change require a different physical response, or just a pattern? That question guides efficient, export-friendly designs.

The Shader Editor is Blender’s node-based environment for building materials. When you select an object and open the Shader Editor, you’ll typically see a Principled BSDF node connected to a Material Output node by default. Think of the Material Output as the final destination for color and surface properties — anything you want to affect the render must connect to it. The power of nodes is that you can insert textures, mix shaders, and add math nodes to control values procedurally. Practically, create a new material from the Material Properties tab or directly within the Shader Editor using the New button. If the object has no material, adding one automatically creates the default Principled BSDF and Material Output pair, so you can start tweaking. A common mistake is editing the wrong object or working in the wrong material slot; always confirm the selected object’s material is active in the editor. For performance, keep node trees as compact as possible for game assets. As an exercise, create a simple node chain: Image Texture → Base Color input of Principled BSDF → Material Output, then preview in Material Preview mode to see immediate results. How would you reduce node complexity for game export?

The Principled BSDF consolidates common physical material controls into a single, intuitive node. Base Color sets the primary tint and is often driven by a texture for detailed surfaces. Metallic is a binary-like property: 0 for non-metals like plastic or wood, 1 for metals like steel; using fractional metallic values on non-metals is a common beginner error and can create physically inconsistent results. Specular controls the intensity of highlights and for PBR workflows it is usually left near the default for non-metals because the shader already models energy-conserving reflections; it has little effect on metals. Roughness governs microfacet spread: low roughness creates sharp, mirror-like reflections, high roughness produces diffuse, matte surfaces. These parameters interact: the same Base Color will read very differently when Metallic flips from 0 to 1 or when Roughness changes from 0.1 to 0.8. When designing for games, tune Roughness to convey material wear and polish, and keep Metallic strictly at 0 or 1 for realistic results. A useful mental model: Base Color = paint, Metallic = material class, Roughness = polish level. Which parameter would you adjust first to turn a matte plastic into a glossy painted car?

Follow a simple process to produce a polished plastic material that reads clearly in material preview. Start by creating a UV Sphere in the 3D Viewport and switching a pane to the Shader Editor. With the sphere selected, click New to create a material — Blender will provide a Principled BSDF connected to Material Output. Set Base Color to a vibrant blue and keep it somewhat saturated so the color reads under different lights. Set Metallic to zero because plastic is a non-metal. Reduce Roughness to about 0.2 to achieve a glossy, polished surface while maintaining subtle micro-variation that prevents a perfect mirror. Leave Specular at the default for PBR consistency. Inspect the result in Material Preview mode, move the viewport light, and notice how reflections sharpen as Roughness decreases. A typical misconception is to push Metallic up to make the highlight brighter — that will change the reflection model and make the surface behave like metal rather than painted plastic. After this exercise, try nudging Roughness slightly to see how much it affects perceived gloss without changing Base Color.

To make a believable brushed metal, start from a duplicated UV sphere so you can compare materials side by side. Create a new material for the duplicate rather than reusing the plastic material. Set Base Color to a dark grey — metals base color is often muted because real metals get their color from reflections rather than diffused pigment. Set Metallic to 1 to ensure the shader uses metal reflection behavior; this is critical because metals reflect the environment and tint reflections by their base color. Increase Roughness to around 0.6 to simulate a brushed surface that scatters reflections while retaining some directional highlights. Optionally add a subtle noise texture into Roughness or Normal input to break uniformity, but be mindful of node complexity for game assets. Remember the common trap: using metallic fractions for non-metals. Metals are typically flagged as fully metallic. After applying these values, move the HDRI or light to see how the object reflects its environment; that reflection behavior is the primary cue that a surface is metallic. How would adding a normal map change the perception of brushed direction?

Create a rough stone material to practice diffuse and high-roughness behavior. Duplicate your sphere again and assign a new material. Set Base Color to a brownish-grey to represent rock, and set Metallic to zero because stone is non-metallic. Increase Roughness to about 0.8 to scatter reflections and give a dull appearance. To add realism, use a texture or procedural noise to modulate the roughness channel so some areas appear slightly shinier where the stone is worn. Normal maps are especially valuable for stone because they add surface detail that catches light at grazing angles. Keep Specular near default for non-metals. A common misconception is that increasing Roughness hides geometry detail — it changes reflections but you still need normal or displacement information to convey bumps and cracks. Inspect the result in Material Preview and rotate the light to verify the surface reads as matte and granular. If you wanted a wet patch, which parameter would you change and in what direction? Hands-on: Create a Rough Stone Material means rough stone: base color earthy, metallic 0, roughness high (~0.8); use normal maps to convey micro-detail.. In practical terms, using roughness and base color for non-metallic, diffuse surfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let’s walk through a compact, practical node setup you will use repeatedly. Start with the Principled BSDF connected to Material Output — that’s the baseline. Add an Image Texture node for Base Color and connect it to Base Color input. For surface detail, add a Normal Map node: load a normal texture into an Image Texture, set its color space to non-color, plug it into the Normal Map node, and connect that into the Principled BSDF Normal input. To vary gloss, add a second Image Texture for Roughness and feed it into the Roughness input. After creating your three materials, run a quick verification checklist to confirm PBR readiness and engine compatibility. First, inspect Base Color textures: ensure they are not overly saturated and that color profiles are correct. Second, check Metallic values: metals should be set to one and non-metals to zero. Third, preview the model under different HDRI setups or lighting rigs to verify reflections and roughness behavior remain plausible. Fourth, open each image texture and set color space correctly — normal maps need non-color, base color should remain sRGB. Fifth, review node complexity: can procedural detail be baked into textures instead of computed in real time? Finally, perform a simple export or bake test: bake base color, normal, and roughness into files and reassign them in a fresh material to compare the baked result with your live nodes. This test tells you whether your material can be simplified for engines. Let’s restate the essential ideas you should carry forward. A material is the collection of properties that control how a surface responds to light; a texture is an image map that provides per-pixel variation. The Principled BSDF is a physically-based shader in Blender designed for predictable, engine-friendly materials. PBR workflows matter because they produce consistent results across lighting conditions and game engines, reducing rework at export. Base Color is the primary tint, Metallic indicates metal or non-metal behavior, Specular tunes highlight intensity and is often left at default for dielectrics, and Roughness controls reflection sharpness. Keep node setups efficient for game assets and always verify color spaces for textures, particularly normal maps. Finally, prefer baking complicated procedural detail to textures when preparing assets for real-time use.
